The Elite Hips are also wireless and offer up to four hours of battery life.
The trade-offs: They’re not a replacement for compression boots. While they provide some relief to your upper quads and hamstrings, their primary focus is the hips and glutes.
Buy if: You regularly struggle with tight hips after activities like running or cycling, or you want to improve hip mobility and range of motion. Honorable Mentions

Urevo’s companion app offers 32 massage modes tailored to different sports and workouts, which is the most I've seen offered in my testing. articles.title: Zuckerberg’s yacht was closer, but someone else saved a stranded boat
articles.text:
Earlier this week, the Alaskan cruise ship Wilderness Legacy rescued a small skiff stranded near Farragut Bay after running out of fuel. But, according to tracking data reviewed by the Alaska Beacon and Halifax Shipping News, the closest vessel was actually Mark Zuckerberg’s super yacht, Launchpad.
Zuckerberg’s yacht was closer, but someone else saved a stranded boat
The small cruise ship Wilderness Legacy rescued the skiff that ran out of fuel.
Michael Love, a passenger on the Wilderness Legacy, posted on Bluesky that the captain announced the Launchpad was closer, but “repeatedly refused to respond,” which was met with booing from the passengers. The AIS tracking (embedded below) seems to support that the Launchpad was closer to the vessel in trouble, but then stopped near the entrance of the bay. The Wilderness Legacy can be seen passing Launchpad, then turning around and towing the stranded boat back to safety.
The US Coast Guard and the Marine Exchange of Alaska did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But Coast Guard Public Affairs Specialist Shannon Shepard told the Alaska Beacon that “at approximately 9:56 p.m., the Coast Guard determined they were not in distress and issued a marine assistance request broadcast on their behalf.”
Brian Baker, spokesperson for Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, told The Verge that “Mark and his family were not on board at the time of the incident. As the Coast Guard noted, the boat was not in distress, and by the time the crew reviewed the Coast Guard contact on a different radio channel from the one they were operating on, the assist was already underway. We’re grateful all parties are safe.”

articles.title: 49ers coach says his Tesla was on Autopilot when he crashed
articles.text:
Four weeks ago, San Francisco 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan was involved in an accident near downtown Palo Alto. At the time Shanahan said only that the accident was his fault. But during a recent press conference he shared more details about the incident, including the fact that he had his Tesla’s Autopilot engaged at the time. Shanahan was not passing the buck, however, saying it was his fault regardless of whether or not Autopilot was engaged.
49ers coach says his Tesla was on Autopilot when he crashed
He still takes responsibility, saying ‘you don’t just turn it [driving] over to a computer.‘
“I’ve had Autopilot for nine years, so I’m pretty comfortable with it and, you know, who knows what happened when I turned around? Whether it malfunctioned or whether I knocked it off? That’s something I don’t know yet. But regardless, that’s… it is always your fault, whether you’re on Autopilot or not. You can’t take your eyes off the road. It’s a partnership driving, you don’t just turn it over to a computer.”
Over the years Tesla’s Autopilot has been linked to hundreds of crashes and dozens of deaths, some of which have resulted in hundreds of millions of dollars in legal settlements.

articles.title: Meetily Lets You Transcribe and Summarize Meetings Without a Subscription—Here’s How
articles.text:
It's perhaps the least hyped, and most useful, feature of the AI age: transcription. As a young journalist, I dreamed of a computer that could turn recordings into text. Now we have that, and it's amazing.
This tech isn't just great for interviews—it's perfect for meetings. A variety of services, called meeting assistants, promise to transcribe and summarize your meetings for you. The appeal here is obvious, but these services don't come cheap or without privacy concerns. Generally, using them means uploading a recording of your meeting to some cloud somewhere, which isn't ideal for projects that require confidentiality. And the tools themselves are generally in the $10 to $20 per month range, price-wise.
Now, as I pointed out with transcription software, the tech for building something like a meeting assistant is open source and widely available for free. Meetily brings it all together in a simple package. Yes, the name is awful, but it uses open-source models, has a great free version, and is available on Windows and macOS (Linux users can build it from source).
Note that there is a Pro version for $10 per month, but the open-source community version is completely free to download from GitHub. Install the application and it will offer to install the models needed. These are the AI tools that do the actual work.
Once those have downloaded, you will need to allow Meetily to record both your microphone's sound and the system audio—that way it can capture all sides of any conversation you're in.
Then you can hit the record button any time you're in a video call. Accessing your microphone and system sound directly means Meetily isn't restricted to specific videoconferencing tools—it'll work with Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and any other service you might come across. You can even theoretically use this for an in-person meeting, assuming your laptop's microphone is capable of picking up sound from everyone in the room. (You may want to look at an AI notetaker if you want a separate device.)
During the meeting, you can watch the transcription take place nearly in real time if you want, or minimize the window and focus on your meeting. When the meeting is done, you can click the stop button, at which point you will see a transcription. From here, you can ask for an AI summary. You can even provide instructions about which points to focus on.
Now, as with all AI tools, there are caveats. These systems aren't perfect, and they may not have the same priorities as you. I intend to write my own meeting minutes using the transcript as a guide, but the meeting summary could still prove useful in certain contexts.
A beta feature allows you to use Meetily with recordings you made previously. This means you can drag an audio or even video file and get a transcript and summary. This is useful if you recorded an in-person conversation on your phone, for example, and want to get a transcript when you're back at your computer.
The free version of Meetily has a few annoying limitations. The transcript can't tell you who said what—no speaker labels—which will be a deal-breaker for many people. I could not find a free and open-source tool that did this consistently, though.
There are a few other similar tools out there if Meetily doesn't work for you. For example, noScribe is a completely free tool that can identify speakers, though it can't record meetings in real time (it only converts files). Anarlog (formerly known as Hyprnote) has an arguably sleeker user interface and access to many AI models, but setup was a bit fiddly compared to Meetily. Quill offers free local transcriptions, but you'll need to sign up for an account to use it (which defeats the point of an offline tool), and there's a lot of upselling.
It's great there are so many free options, and if this field is anything like dictation software, I'm sure there will be even more in a few months.

articles.title: Bỏ phố về quê nuôi ngỗng, người đàn ông xây đế chế gan ngỗng thách thức Pháp
articles.text:
Năm 15 tuổi, Lý Phong Sơn đã thấm thía cái đói khi cả gia đình chỉ có đủ gạo cho một bữa ăn duy nhất mỗi ngày.
Ba thập kỷ sau, ông lái chiếc Maserati ngang qua những cánh đồng mênh mông ở miền Đông Trung Quốc. Ở đó, 400.000 con ngỗng đang được chăm sóc để tạo ra thứ gan béo ngậy từng là đặc sản độc quyền của người Pháp.
Đến nay, ông Lý đã xây dựng một cơ ngơi khổng lồ từ nghề nuôi ngỗng lấy gan, đặc sản vốn là thế mạnh của người Pháp. Năm 2025, công ty Trường Hào của ông sản xuất 300 tấn gan ngỗng. Năm nay, con số này dự kiến cán mốc 500 tấn. Trong khi đó, một trang trại điển hình tại Pháp chỉ đạt trung bình 10 tấn/năm.
Câu chuyện của ông không chỉ là hành trình vượt lên số phận, mà còn phản ánh cách Trung Quốc từng bước soán ngôi số 1 toàn cầu của Pháp trong ngành công nghiệp gan ngỗng.
Bí quyết tạo nên lợi thế của ngành gan ngỗng Trung Quốc
Trong 10 năm qua, gan ngỗng tại Trung Quốc đã chuyển mình từ một món ăn xa xỉ dành cho giới thượng lưu thành sản phẩm phổ biến với giá phải chăng.
Sản lượng nước này được ước tính đạt khoảng 14.000 tấn vào năm ngoái, tăng gấp 7 lần so với mức 2.000 tấn một thập kỷ trước. Trong khi đó, Pháp - nhà sản xuất hàng đầu thế giới, lại ghi nhận sản lượng giảm nhẹ xuống còn khoảng 15.044 tấn. Hai quốc gia hiện chiếm hơn 80% sản lượng toàn cầu.
Chủ tịch Hiệp hội Gan ngỗng Pháp (CIFOG), ông Fabien Chevalier thừa nhận: "Họ phát triển nhanh đến mức đáng lo ngại. Chúng tôi không ngờ tốc độ tiến tới của họ lại nhanh như vậy".
Sự bùng nổ sản lượng của Trung Quốc đến từ sự kết hợp của nhiều yếu tố. Đầu tiên là sự hỗ trợ mạnh mẽ từ chính phủ: các khoản trợ cấp chiếm hơn 50% chi phí cơ sở hạ tầng và vắc-xin cho trang trại của ông Lý.
Thứ hai là quy trình sản xuất công nghiệp hóa với cường độ làm việc cao. Mỗi nhân viên tại trang trại của ông Lý phụ trách hơn 400 con ngỗng.
Trong 10 ngày cuối của chu kỳ nuôi kéo dài 100 ngày, họ làm việc gần như không ngừng nghỉ để vỗ béo mỗi con tới 6 bữa/ngày. Ông Lý giải thích: "Người châu Âu hiện không còn duy trì được các trang trại ngỗng quy mô lớn, vì đó là công việc vất vả".
Nhờ quy trình này, gan của mỗi con ngỗng tại trang trại của ông nặng ít nhất 1kg và có thể lên tới 2,9kg. Trong khi đó, tại Pháp, gan vịt điển hình chỉ nặng 500-550 gram, còn gan ngỗng thường dưới 750 gram.
Chưa dừng ở quy trình hiện tại, ông Lý còn đang hợp tác với các công ty robot để tự động hóa quá trình nuôi và ép ăn, nhằm giảm bớt lao động thủ công.
Câu chuyện từ ‘thủ phủ’ gan ngỗng
Tại huyện Lâm Cù, tỉnh Sơn Đông, nơi sản xuất 70% thị trường nội địa và 20% sản lượng gan ngỗng toàn cầu, quy mô ngành tại đây còn gây ấn tượng mạnh hơn.
Lâm Cù bắt đầu nuôi ngỗng từ năm 1988, khi doanh nghiệp nhà nước tiên phong nhập khẩu hàng nghìn con ngỗng Lang Đức từ Pháp.
Để giúp giống ngỗng này thích nghi, vào những năm 1990, doanh nghiệp Trung Quốc đã mời chuyên gia người Pháp sang đào tạo suốt 3 năm với mức lương lên tới 150.000 NDT/tháng (khoảng 580 triệu đồng), chưa kể chi phí xe, phiên dịch và khách sạn.
Công ty Tôn Thuận tại đây đã phát triển máy cho ăn bán tự động thế hệ thứ 5 với cảm biến thông minh, giúp tăng hiệu quả sản xuất lên gấp 5 lần.
Nhờ công nghệ, họ biến gan ngỗng thành hàng loạt sản phẩm mới: gan ngỗng rượu vang đỏ, gan ngỗng kem, với hương vị anh đào, việt quất, rượu trắng...
Tổng giám đốc Xuân Quán (Chunguan Food), bà Mã Lập Quân, cho biết công ty đã phát triển hơn 60 sản phẩm từ gan ngỗng, như gan tươi, gan sốt rượu vang đến các loại ăn liền. Nhờ đổi mới sản phẩm, doanh thu công ty tăng vọt từ 3 tỷ NDT (khoảng 11.600 tỷ đồng) lên 4 tỷ NDT (khoảng 15.400 tỷ đồng) chỉ trong vòng một năm.
Một lát gan ngỗng tại nhà hàng Trung Quốc có giá từ 30-70 NDT (khoảng 116.000-270.000 đồng), rẻ hơn nhiều so với mức 15-40 euro (450.000-1,2 triệu đồng) tại Pháp. Giá thấp giúp nhu cầu nội địa tăng mạnh, đồng thời tạo lợi thế cạnh tranh khi thâm nhập các thị trường mới.
Mặc dù hiện chưa tới 5% sản lượng được xuất khẩu do các quy định kiểm dịch nghiêm ngặt của Trung Quốc (yêu cầu kiểm tra 300 loại hóa chất) nhưng các doanh nghiệp nước này đang từng bước mở rộng thị trường.
Ngành gan ngỗng toàn cầu đang chứng kiến một cuộc chuyển giao quyền lực thầm lặng. Chỉ trong khoảng một thập kỷ, gan ngỗng tại Trung Quốc đã từ món ăn xa xỉ trở thành thực phẩm phổ biến với mức giá dễ tiếp cận hơn.
Theo Baidu

articles.title: How to use Claude's voice mode - Engadget
articles.text:
How to use Claude's voice mode
Anthropic's chatbot can be very vocal, if you want it to be.
Since 2025, Anthropic has offered a voice mode through Claude, allowing you to speak to its chatbot instead of writing out your prompts. This past July, the company updated the feature to make it more useful. Before, voice mode limited users to speaking to Claude through Haiku, Anthropic's least powerful model. This was done to reduce latency. Now, voice mode also works through the company's more powerful models, including Sonnet and Opus, and can even pull context from your connected apps and services.
If you're a frequent Claude user and want to give the feature a try, here's how to do it.
How to use Claude voice
Voice mode is available through the Claude mobile (Android and iOS) and desktop apps, as well as through the web. Anthropic says the feature works best from your phone.
To use voice mode on mobile:
- 
Open the Claude app.
- 
Tap the black waveform icon in the lower right corner of the interface (not the microphone icon right next to it).
- 
Grant the app microphone permissions if necessary.
- 
Start talking. Claude will generate a response once you finish a prompt.
- 
Claude will remain in voice mode until you tap Stop.
One thing to keep in mind is Claude's voice mode uses a "turn-based" architecture, meaning the chatbot will listen to you before it generates a response. This is different from ChatGPT's voice mode, which OpenAI recently updated to use a "duplex" architecture. That system gives its GPT-Live models the ability to simultaneously process speech and generate outputs.
In practice, that means voice mode sometimes confuses a brief pause for the end of a question or prompt. For that reason, Anthropic recommends asking multi-part questions one at a time instead of all at once.
How to select different models
You can change the model Claude will use to generate a response from the model picker at the bottom of the interface. See below for a list of available models, followed by a short description from Anthropic.
- 
Haiku: Fastest for quick answers
- 
Sonnet: Most efficient for everyday tasks
- 
Opus: For complex tasks. Only available to paid accounts.
How to use your connected apps
Like with text chat, voice mode can access apps and services you've connected to Claude, including Gmail, Google Calendar and Slack. For example, you can ask Claude to summarize your recent emails. Simply tell Claude the app you want it to use as part of a prompt. If you're accessing a third-party app for the first time, you will need to grant Claude permission to use it.
How to change Claude's voice and language
As of July 2026, Anthropic offers Voice Mode support in 14 different languages, with a handful of those available in additional dialects. The language you select will affect your choice of Claude's voice. In English, for instance, you can select from five different options, while Japanese users are limited to just two. Below is the full list of languages Voice Mode currently supports:
- 
English
- 
English (India)
- 
English (United Kingdom)
- 
Chinese (Simplified)
- 
Cantonese
- 
French
- 
French (Canada)
- 
German
- 
German (Austria)
- 
Hindi
- 
Italian
- 
Japanese
- 
Korean
- 
Portuguese
- 
Portuguese (Brazil)
- 
Portuguese (Portugal)
- 
Russian
- 
Spanish
- 
Spanish (Latin America)
- 
Turkish
- 
Ukrainian
One limitation of Voice Mode is that Claude cannot detect if switch between languages mid-sentence. If you're about to speak in another language, state that intent out loud, or change Claude's language from the Settings menu.
To change Claude's voice and language, open the Settings page and tap Voice (located below the App section of the menu). You can hear a preview of each by swiping through the carousel at the top. In English, you have the following options:
- 
Buttery
- 
Airy
- 
Mellow
- 
Glassy
- 
Rounded
Additionally, you can also adjust the speed of Claude's cadence. There, your options are Slow, Normal and Fast. Lastly, Anthropic offers two different ways of recording your prompts: Hands free and Push to talk. Anthropic suggests the former is best used in quiet environments.
Do you need a paid account to use Claude Voice?
You don't need to pay for a Pro or Max subscription to access Claude Voice, but Anthropic limits free accounts to using the tool through its Haiku and Sonnet models. For most prompts, Sonnet should offer more than enough intelligence. To route your prompts through Anthropic's more Opus powerful model, a paid subscription is required. Voice mode conversations count against your usage limits.
Anthropic also limits free accounts to a single connection, though you can use the tool in all the languages it currently supports.

articles.title: TCL Note A1 Nxtpaper Review: A Hybrid Tablet for Taking Notes and Watching Video
articles.text:
Nice high-res matte screen. Excellent pen with good pressure sensitivity. Good handwriting conversion tools. Works well as an ebook reader. Great for watching video.
TIRED
Keyboard case adds unnecessary bulk. Lacks hardware volume buttons. User interface feels like a work in progress. Writing onscreen isn't as nice as on E Ink devices.
Tablets are secondary devices for most of us, but there's one place where they outshine laptops: digital note-taking. Attempting to bridge the gap between analog and digital, digital notebooks offer a paper-like writing experience with all the pros of digital notes.
ReMarkable devices are probably the best known in this space, and they top our digital notebook guide, but I've always wanted something a little more versatile—what if I want to stream a baseball game on the same device I take notes on? E Ink, the technology employed by digital notebooks and e-readers, isn't the best choice in that case.
TCL's Note A1 Nxtpaper tablet uses a more traditional, though still matte, tablet screen to get as close to the E Ink writing experience as possible, while still being able to display video when you want to expand beyond just taking notes. It mostly works, but it can't completely mimic the feel of writing on paper, and there are a few quirks with the user interface.
Hybrid Screen
The heart of any digital notebook is the screen—how well does it mimic paper? With E Ink, the answer is pretty darn well, but this is not actually E Ink. TCL's Note A1 Nxtpaper is built around a custom 1440 x 2200-pixel matte LCD panel with a 120-Hz refresh rate. At first glance, it looks like E Ink, and indeed it reduces glare and is easier on the eye than a typical tablet. At the same time, it's still an LCD panel capable of the color rendering and responsiveness of a traditional Android tablet. (The Nxtpaper matte LCD technology is proprietary to TCL.)
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
It's not E Ink, but I find the Note A1 screen to be quite nice and a perfectly acceptable alternative given how much more versatile it is than an E Ink screen. However, if what you love about E Ink note-taking devices is the paperlike experience, this is not the device for you (I'll explain more in the next section). It's certainly much nicer to look at and to write on than a typical glossy Android tablet.
While it is not perfect, the Note A1's screen feels very close to the hybrid note-taking/true tablet device that I've been searching for—one part real screen, one part writing pad.
The rest of the tablet is about what you'd expect in a midrange to high-end Android tablet. There's a MediaTek G100 processor, with 8 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage. That's enough power to run all the apps I tested and power some of the AI-driven features TCL is pushing with this device, including automated meeting summaries, audio-to-text transcription, and, of course, handwriting-to-text conversion.
All this is wrapped in a solid aluminum body that's almost exactly the same size and weight as the 11-inch Kindle Scribe. The Note A1 is 5 millimeters thick and weighs 500 grams.
I have two gripes with the Note A1 hardware. The first is the keyboard case, which is unnecessarily heavy and complicated. TCL apparently hired an origami expert to design the keyboard case, which has three panels where two usually does the job. The result is a keyboard case that adds an annoying level of weight, thickness, and complexity where none of that is required. For all that though, the keyboard itself is quite nice to type on. The other problem is the lack of hardware volume buttons. Volume buttons are good, mmmkay?
Writing, Drawing, Reading
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
Besides the screen, the bundled T-Pen Pro is the highlight of this tablet. The fact that it's bundled is somewhat unusual these days, as many manufacturers have followed Apple's lead and made their writing devices a separate purchase.
This isn't some throwaway pen either; it's very good, with excellent pressure sensitivity and extremely low latency, which makes writing with it feel a lot more natural than some tablets I've tested.
But the overall writing experience doesn't feel like paper. Devices like the ReMarkable have spent a lot of effort getting the texture and feel of paper into the screen-writing experience. The A1 Note can't compete on this front because it still feels like writing on a glass tablet. This didn't bother me as I've never really wanted to replicate the exact feel of paper notebooks on digital (if I want to write on paper, I, well, write on paper), but if you're coming from a device like the ReMarkable, know that the writing experience here is more like a traditional tablet screen.
Despite this, the pen is really nice for taking notes, annotating documents, and even sketching. There are several tips available, and you can customize the pen quite a bit, including setting up custom shortcuts. There's also good handwriting and shape recognition tools in the A1 Note's note-taking software.
The Note A1 supports a broad range of document formats, from PDF docs to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, EPUB, MOBI, AZW3 (Kindle), and more. That means you aren't locked into any specific reader or app on the device.
Similarly for syncing, you can use whatever you like. TCL ships with Google's Play Store installed, but I had no trouble downloading and installing F-Droid, then installing Syncthing and some open-source apps that I use. That said, at times, I felt like I was fighting against the UI that TCL developed for the Note A1.
The device, despite running Android, has a UI designed for note-taking. There's a sidebar that gives you access to any apps you install (more on that below). At the top of the screen is a short to-do list and the Inspiration Space, which is like a free-form clipboard area where you can store things you want to highlight (pretty much anything, which is very useful). Below that, you have your list of notes.
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
Click on a note with the pen, and it will open in edit mode with a configuration toolbar shown across the top. Here you can set up pen type, color, line thickness, and all the other tools you'd want to use to write or draw. I found the editing interface just about perfect in the sense that it balances keeping it simple but still giving you access to the controls you actually need.
The other element I enjoyed in the Note A1 UI is the Inspiration Space. I can easily clip a bit of text from any document (including web pages), save it, and then automatically convert it to text for use in something else or apply any of the other onboard AI-powered tools. It's one of the best clip-and-save tools I've used since I gave up on Evernote.
What I was less thrilled with is the file management system. It works, but there are confusing shortcomings. For example, I couldn't find a way to open a note in reading mode and then switch to editing from within the note. This seems like a very common use case. But no, you have to exit the note, go back to the main notes menu, and then reopen it in editing mode.
The interface is not very intuitive. I had to consult the manual to figure out how to get two documents open side-by-side, something that works by drag and drop in every other Android device I've tested (even those with highly customized UIs).
A Note on Earlier Versions
Curiously for a large publicly traded company, TCL launched the Note A1 via Kickstarter (but clearly already had plenty of the tablet available, which the company fed to YouTube influencers). If you hunt down early reviews of these Kickstarter devices, you'll notice people complaining about limited app availability, no Google Play Store, and having to sideload apps via F-Droid, the Aurora Store, and other shenanigans.
The Note A1 I tested, and the device that is for sale these days at all major retailers, comes with the Google Play Store preinstalled, making it easy to download any app you need. Accessing installed apps can be a little awkward; they pile up in the sidebar menu, but if you make good use of the ability to customize the launcher, it's not too difficult to have everything you need close at hand. And for completeness sake, I did install F-Droid and the Aurora Store, and both also work (although if Google carries through with its current development plans for Android, apps installed with F-Droid will stop working on all Android devices next year).
Competition
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
There are two competitors here. The first is an E Ink tablet. If you want the most paperlike possible experience, then the E Ink wins. But you won't be watching videos or perusing social media. If you want 80 percent of the E Ink experience, but also the ability to use your device as a normal Android tablet, then the Note A1 is the clear winner.
The other major competitor here is TCL itself, namely the Nxtpaper 11 Plus, which offers much of the same experience, albeit with a less powerful chip, costs half the price, and doesn't have the same custom UI. Most compellingly, the Nxtpaper 11 Plus is regularly on sale for less than half the price of the Note A1 Nxtpaper. While you do get a nicer, more powerful piece of hardware in the Note A1, I'm not sure it's twice as nice.
While the Note A1 is not perfect, for the right person it's pretty close. The screen is excellent and paperlike enough for most people, and writing and drawing are great. The keyboard, though deeply flawed, works fine, while the software is 90 percent of the way there; encouragingly, TCL seems to be updating it based on feedback. As with all TCL devices, the support period is on the short side, but given the level of Android customization here, I don't think that's unreasonable. If you've been looking for an E Ink–like device that's more versatile, this is the best hybrid tablet I've tested.
Scott Gilbertson is Operations Manager for the WIRED Reviews Team. He was previously a writer and editor for WIRED’s Webmonkey.com, covering the independent web and early internet culture. You can reach him at luxagraf.net. ... Read More

articles.title: Dropbox is a PC builder’s best friend
articles.text:
In 2018 I bet my reputation and self-worth on a huge crowdfunded game design project. It could have been a failure for many reasons, but the one I became most worried about was losing all of the work that was stored locally on my home-built PC — a scenario that would have left a lot of people very upset and placed me in deep trouble. I wasn’t irresponsible, I had local backups, but at some point I found myself in custody of so many important files that it scared me. And no matter how many redundancies I could build at home, they’d all still be in the same place — a risky bet. So I bought a subscription to Dropbox. Years later, it’s still one of the best software subscriptions that I happily renew each year.
Dropbox is a PC builder’s best friend
When catastrophe strikes, having your whole computer in the cloud makes recovery a breeze.
It was great to have all that work backed up in the cloud — both for peace of mind and because it made working with collaborators breezier, letting them upload stuff directly to my drive, and letting me transfer files up to 50GB in size. In quick order I had built a trove of incredible artwork and complicated InDesign, Photoshop, and Illustrator files. The original goal for my Dropbox configuration was to make sure I wouldn’t lose any data in a worst-case scenario, so I set it up to mirror everything living on my work partition. Eventually, I ran smack into a worst-case scenario. Not once, but twice.
I’m still not sure why, but my latest home-built PC chewed through two separate 2TB Samsung 970 Evo SSDs. It’s difficult to tell what went wrong with them, but in each case I woke up one morning to find when I tried to boot up that no drive could be detected. I can still feel my stomach trying to sink into the floor when I press that power button these days, never knowing if my drive had died in its sleep.
Fortunately, both times, after some process-of-elimination testing I learned that just the drive had gone bad and everything else in my system was A-OK. Maybe I should have ditched Samsung after the second disaster, but I’m now on an 2TB 990 Evo Plus. Knock on wood, this thing better not fail. That drive now costs almost twice what I originally paid for it thanks to our new outrageously priced world of parts.
My Dropbox bill is about $204 a year for a family plan ($17 a month), which includes up to six members. If you’re just in it for yourself you can get it for $9.99 a month billed yearly (about $120 a year), which comes with 2TB of storage. You can upgrade to 3TB for around $143 a year. That might be a tough sell for people who already have dozens of subscriptions, but I find it to be a decent price for excellent digital insurance.
There are other powerful options out there, especially for professionals working with heavy files or complicated workflows. Backblaze, for example, has a personal backup plan with unlimited data for $99 a year and no restrictions on file size. And, of course, if you live on the Mac, Apple iCloud Plus isn’t a bad option — especially if you’re already paying for an Apple One subscription. Even Adobe offers file backups through Creative Cloud if that’s your jam, but I would not recommend using that clunky software suite for anything other than doing the work you need to do.
I can’t recall a single time the service failed
I prefer Dropbox because the software works consistently well across multiple operating systems and is usually neither seen nor heard. The Windows client is snappy and I’ve found with a fast internet connection that its real-time syncing is efficient and painless. Anytime a file is modified in the partition I have mirrored in the cloud, Dropbox quietly begins uploading it and making changes to my mirrored files in the cloud. After using it for about eight years now I can’t recall a single time the service failed or faltered. It’s so fast and reliable I often forget it’s even there.
Now, for the important caveat: This might not work for you if you have poor internet speeds. It really depends on how much data you’re regularly moving around on your computer and how quickly you make changes to it. This could particularly be a problem for asymmetrical data plans that commonly boast lightning-fast download speeds while offering pathetic upload speeds. I’ve done fine averaging only about 20Mbps upload, but if you’re on something even lower you should try a free trial for a backup plan before committing. You can also find plenty of download time calculators online; at my gigabit download speed it usually takes around two hours to download the 1TB of files I have synced in the cloud.
And one more caveat: Putting everything (or even just many things) on your computer in the cloud isn’t for everyone, and I completely understand why many folks wouldn’t or shouldn’t do that for sensitive files. I once built local RAID drives and even airgapped storage systems to avoid having everything online. These things are still possible but getting more expensive by the day as storage prices spike. You’re the best judge of how and where your data should be protected.
That sinking feeling of potentially losing my whole PC? It was immediately followed each time by the assurance that I’d only lost a computer’s body and not its soul. When I got my PC back up and running with new storage, it ended up taking less time to resync all my files than it did to troubleshoot and install new hardware. I can almost hear Billy Crudup doing a Mastercard commercial in my head: New solid state drive, three hundred eighty-nine dollars. Yearly Dropbox subscription, two hundred and three dollars. Never worrying about losing your data? Priceless.

articles.title: Gần nửa triệu tấn thịt nhập khẩu đổ bộ thị trường, giá rẻ bất ngờ
articles.text:
Theo thống kê sơ bộ từ Cục Hải quan, nhập khẩu thịt và các sản phẩm từ thịt của Việt Nam trong quý II/2026 đạt 271,1 nghìn tấn, trị giá ước gần 810,1 triệu USD, tăng 21,5% về lượng và tăng 24,1% về giá trị so với quý I liền kề.
Còn so với quý II/2025, nhập khẩu nhóm mặt hàng thực phẩm này tăng 14,4% về lượng và tăng tới 46,9% về giá trị.
Lũy kế 6 tháng đầu năm 2026, nhập khẩu thịt và các sản phẩm từ thịt của Việt Nam đạt 494,3 nghìn tấn, trị giá khoảng 1,46 tỷ USD, tăng 9,6% về lượng và tăng 36,4% về giá trị so với cùng kỳ năm 2025.
Số liệu thống kê cũng cho thấy, nước ta chủ yếu nhập khẩu các loại thịt và phụ phẩm ăn được sau giết mổ của gia cầm; phụ phẩm ăn được sau giết mổ của lợn, trâu, bò sống; thịt trâu tươi, ướp lạnh hoặc đông lạnh; thịt lợn tươi, ướp lạnh hoặc đông lạnh; thịt bò tươi, ướp lạnh hoặc đông lạnh...
Đáng chú ý, dù cước vận tải biển trong nửa đầu năm nay tăng cao do ảnh hưởng bởi xung đột địa chính trị trên thế giới, song giá bình quân thịt nhập khẩu lại tương đối rẻ, chỉ khoảng 2,95 USD/kg (tương đương khoảng 77.500 đồng/kg.). Mức giá này thấp hơn nhiều so với giá các sản phẩm thịt trong nước sản xuất.
Khi nguồn cung nhập khẩu và sản lượng thịt nội địa đều tăng, trong khi sức mua vẫn còn yếu đã kéo theo giá nhiều sản phẩm chăn nuôi trong nước giảm về mức thấp.
Báo cáo của Bộ Nông nghiệp và Môi trường (NN&MT) cho thấy, giá thu mua lợn hơi trong nước biến động giảm trong tháng 7 vừa qua. Cụ thể, giá lợn hơi tại miền Bắc giảm 3.500 đồng/kg so với tháng 6, xuống 62.000-64.000 đồng/kg; ở miền Trung - Tây Nguyên giảm 3.000 đồng/kg, chỉ còn 60.000-62.000 đồng/kg; trong khi tại miền Nam giá là 60.000-62.000 đồng/kg, giảm 1.000 đồng/kg.
Theo cập nhật mới nhất, mặt bằng giá lợn hơi toàn quốc đã giảm về 58.000-62.000 đồng/kg. Các doanh nghiệp cho rằng đây là mức giá thấp nhất kể từ đầu năm.
“Giá lợn hơi giảm do áp lực từ nguồn cung khá dồi dào và sức mua chưa cải thiện”, Bộ NN&MT chỉ rõ trong báo cáo.
Báo cáo kết quả sản xuất và thương mại gia cầm trong 6 tháng đầu năm 2026 của Hiệp hội Gia cầm Việt Nam cũng cho thấy, kim ngạch nhập khẩu thịt gà và phụ phẩm tăng mạnh so với cùng kỳ năm 2025.
Cùng với đó, do tổng đàn tăng trưởng nhanh từ cuối năm 2025 kéo dài sang đầu năm nay khiến tình trạng dư cung diễn ra trên diện rộng. Trong đó, phân khúc gà công nghiệp lông trắng nuôi ngắn ngày bị tác động mạnh nhất. Đặc biệt, tại khu vực phía Nam, giá loại gà công nghiệp này có thời điểm giảm mạnh xuống 22.000-24.000 đồng/kg, thấp hơn giá thành sản xuất.
Giá gà lông màu nuôi dài ngày dù vẫn giữ mức tăng nhẹ so với đầu năm, song vẫn thấp hơn cùng kỳ năm ngoái.
Trong tháng 7 vừa qua, giá gà ở nước ta tiếp tục biến động. Theo đó, gà lông màu giá dao động từ 47.000-48.000 đồng/kg; gà công nghiệp có giá trong khoảng 32.000-35.000 đồng/kg.
Giám đốc một doanh nghiệp chăn nuôi cho rằng nguồn cung thịt lợn, thịt gà đang dồi dào nhưng sức mua vẫn yếu, cộng với áp lực từ nguồn hàng nhập khẩu giá rẻ đã kéo giá sản phẩm trong nước giảm thêm.
Trong bối cảnh giá thức ăn chăn nuôi neo cao, giá thịt lợn và thịt gà ở mức thấp, lợi nhuận của người nuôi có nguy cơ bị thu hẹp, thậm chí thua lỗ nếu năng suất không đạt kỳ vọng, vị này nhấn mạnh.

articles.title: The 12 Best Anime to Watch if You Think You Hate Anime
articles.text:
Despite its ferocious popularity, people still tend to swear off anime entirely. These are usually the people whose reference of the medium pertains to a certain stereotype or to the few seconds of anime they once saw on a computer somewhere in the early 2000s.
But Japan has been producing some of the most emotionally resonant and visually audacious storytelling in contemporary media for half a century, and a great deal of it looks nothing at all like the stereotype it holds.
So here’s a case for the uninitiated. Start with self-contained films you can knock out in a single evening before graduating to series worth committing wholly to. The common thread, if you’re keeping score, is that not one of these requires you to know anything about anime, or Japan for that matter, going in.
Note that many of these picks are available in both the original Japanese audio with subtitles or as “dubs” with dialog dubbed by English voice actors. Dive in however you’d like.
Solo Leveling
If you want something fast, slick and unapologetically addictive, start here. Adapted from a South Korean web novel and webtoon by the Japanese animation studio A-1 Pictures, Solo Leveling follows Sung Jinwoo, an E-rank hunter regarded as the weakest of his profession. After being slaughtered during a dungeon expedition, he awakens with access to a mysterious system that only he can see–and which allows him to become stronger in a world where everyone else’s abilities are effectively fixed. Watching him transform from expendable underdog into an overwhelmingly powerful fighter is pure wish fulfillment, driven by propulsive pacing and enormous battles.
The Girl Who Leapt Through Time
This 2006 film is one of the softest possible landings into anime, with a concept that is simple to follow. Makoto is an ordinary teenager who unexpectedly discovers that she can leap backward through time. She initially uses the ability to redo poor test results, avoid awkward confessions, and correct everyday embarrassments. But manipulating time has consequences for the people around her, forcing Makoto to confront a future she may not be able to reverse.
Frieren: Beyond Journey’s End
Most fantasy stories end when the heroes defeat the great evil. Frieren begins there. After completing a decade-long quest, the elven mage takes off on a solitary journey, returning after 50 years to find that her human companions have aged while she has remained unchanged. Regret at missing out on reconnecting earlier and the pain of witnessing the death of one of her friends sets her on a journey of self-discovery. The result is a quiet, beautifully animated meditation on memory, mortality, and the meaning we find in seemingly fleeting relationships.
Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind
Take a trip back to the anime of the ’80s, when writer-director Hayao Miyazaki was helping redefine what Japanese animation could accomplish—even before he cofounded Studio Ghibli. Set in a world poisoned by ecological catastrophe, the film follows Princess Nausicaä as she tries to prevent a war between human kingdoms while understanding the enormous toxic forest spreading across the planet. It is a postapocalyptic adventure but also a remarkably prescient story about environmental destruction and humanity’s impulse to conquer what it fears.
Death Note
For viewers who think anime means sprawling fights and exaggerated superpowers, Death Note offers a psychological thriller instead. High school student Light Yagami discovers a supernatural notebook that allows him to kill anyone whose name he writes inside it, provided he knows their face. With this discovery, he launches a crusade to eliminate criminals. What follows is a compulsive, morally murky battle of wits about justice, power, and how quickly idealism can become tyranny.
The Colors Within
Totsuko is a Catholic girls’ school student with an ability to see people’s emotions as colors. She joins a band with two people whose auras she’s drawn to, and so unfolds a musical odyssey of emotion and connection, tuned to classic anime characteristics. This 2024 Japanese drama film is a great watch if you’re after something with a bit more depth.
Jujutsu Kaisen
For anyone who wants supernatural horror with spectacular action, Jujutsu Kaisen is an easy gateway. High school student Yuji Itadori swallows a cursed finger to save a classmate and becomes the vessel of Ryomen Sukuna, a reincarnated sorcerer known as the King of Curses. Yuji is brought into the secretive world of jujutsu sorcerers, who fight supernatural beings created from humanity’s negative emotions. The series becomes considerably darker as it progresses, but its humor, memorable characters, and inventive battles make the commitment worthwhile.
The Tale of the Princess Kaguya
Japan’s most famous folklore reimagined in a hand-drawn masterpiece by Isao Takahata took eight years to make. As if sketched in real time, the story unfolds with a bamboo cutter who discovers a tiny girl inside a stalk. He raises her and watches her transform into a woman of impossible beauty. But the girl is slowly suffocated by everyone else’s plans for her, including five noble suitors competing for her hand.
Kiki’s Delivery Service
Even if you have never explored anime, you have probably encountered this one. Hayao Miyazaki’s 1989 fantasy follows Kiki, a 13-year-old witch who leaves home as part of her training and settles in a seaside city with her talking cat, Jiji. She begins supporting herself by running an airborne delivery service, only to find her confidence—and her ability to fly—beginning to disappear. Ostensibly a children’s film, it is also an unusually perceptive story about independence, loneliness, and creative burnout.
Spirited Away
Hayao Miyazaki’s 2001 masterpiece remains one of the strongest arguments for animation as serious cinema. Ten-year-old Chihiro unknowingly enters a mysterious spirit world where her parents eat food at an abandoned amusement park and are transformed into pigs. She then finds work in a magical bathhouse as she searches for a way to save them.
Strange, frightening, and intensely imaginative, the film refuses to explain every corner of its world. Instead, it trusts viewers to follow Chihiro through a story about courage, greed and growing up. In 2003, it became the first non-English-language film to win the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.
Fruits Basket
Developed from its Japanese manga origin to a full animated series in 2019, Fruits Basket is a wild story of a generational curse spanning three seasons. The Soma family has a strange secret. If any of them embrace, they transform into animals of the Chinese zodiac. By its final season, it earns catharsis as much as it does a fanbase of emotionally invested devotees. Hulu has the English dubbed version, and Crunchyroll has both the dubbed and subtitled versions.
Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba
If you find yourself somewhat tempted by anime that’s got swords and demons, this is an adventure series for you. It is also one of the biggest animation phenomenons of the decade, with movie spinoffs that have broken box office records. Main character Tanjiro embarks on a wild journey to avenge a demon attack on his family, unfolding over four seasons of thrilling plot lines and impressive hand-drawn fight sequences.
This story was originally published by WIRED Middle East.

articles.title: Here's how to format a USB drive on Windows - Engadget
articles.text:
Here's how to format a USB drive on Windows
And why you might need to.
Knowing how to format a storage drive is a crucial bit of knowledge for any computer user. It's a common misconception that formatting is only for wiping a drive that's full of files you no longer need. Whether you find a drive that's simply not compatible with your operating system, or have the displeasure of encountering corrupted data, formatting sets your storage device back to a like-new state and wipes the slate clean.
Formatting a drive doesn't just mean wiping it clean of stored data. It also means overwriting sectors so previously stored data cannot be recovered, setting the file system up anew, and scanning for bad sectors. It's always a good idea to format a USB drive before reusing it, even if you've deleted all the files previously stored on it. Formatting will wipe out any latent ghost files, clear out any hidden malware (you never know!) and optimize the drive for stability.
But what many people don't know is that you should also format a brand new drive before using it. USB drives of all kinds come from the factory with configurations that support broad compatibility but may not match your specific needs. Flash drives in particular, from brands like SanDisk, Kingston and so on, tend to come configured with an older file storage format called FAT32, which has broad compatibility but cannot handle files larger than a few gigabytes.
Whatever your reason for formatting, it can seem daunting until you get the hang of it. So, here's how to format a USB drive on Windows, and how to know which settings to choose when doing so.
What's the best storage format for Windows (and other devices you own)?
There are three main storage formats for a drive you'll use externally with a Windows system. Windows itself uses NTFS for internal drives due to its support for partitioning and encryption, among other things. If you plan on using your USB 2.0 or 3.0 drive exclusively with Windows systems, NTFS is the best choice. However, you should not use NTFS if there's a chance you'll be plugging your drive into a Linux, Android, iOS or macOS system.
For non-Windows operating systems, the storage format with the broadest compatibility is exFAT. It can handle large files of more than 4GB, so if you plan on using the drive to gain more storage on your Android phone, or to store movies and 4K videos, compressed archives, and so on, exFAT is the de facto choice. While it lacks some of the more advanced features supported by NTFS, it is well suited to thumb drives and basic portable SSDs.
You may also notice an option labeled FAT32, which is the older version of the format. If you foresee using your drive with an older device like a car stereo or ancient printer, FAT32 has the most compatibility of any format and works with just about anything that has a USB port. However, it has serious limitations that render it a bad option for modern use cases. It cannot support files larger than 4GB and is more prone to fragmentation than newer formats. Windows 11 may not play nice with it, either, depending on your use case.
How to properly format your storage drive for Windows
The actual process of formatting the drive is pretty simple. Just plug the USB storage device into a high-speed USB port, then open Windows Explorer. Click This PC on the left-hand navigation panel, then right-click the drive and select Format. Be sure you're selecting the correct drive, and that you have closed any programs that might still be using the drive or any files on it.
The Windows formatting tool offers a number of different file formats, which can be selected from the second dropdown menu. As discussed above, choose exFAT if you plan to use the USB drive with non-Windows devices such as Android phones, Linux computers or Macs and iPhones. If you'll exclusively use it with Windows, you can choose NTFS.
You can leave file allocation set to the default, which for most modern USB drives is either 32KB or 128KB when formatting to exFAT. If you plan on using the drive exclusively for storing large files, like games, you can choose a higher value, and you can choose a lower one if you have a lot of very small files like text notes. As a rule of thumb, the larger the drive is and the larger the files you want to store, the larger you can make the allocation size.
Under Volume Label, enter a custom name for the drive, if you want one.
Click Format, and then click OK on the confirmation that appears. Depending on the size of the drive and how full it is, formatting can take anywhere from a couple of seconds to several minutes. Another pop-up will appear once formatting is complete. Confirm and close out of the formatting tool, and you should now have a freshly formatted USB drive.

articles.title: AI detectors are creating a new era of distrust
articles.text:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more news about how AI is changing our daily lives, follow Emma Roth. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
AI detectors are creating a new era of distrust
Tools that promise to detect AI writing can be dubious, but educators and publishers are using them anyway.
AI detectors are creating a new era of distrust
Tools that promise to detect AI writing can be dubious, but educators and publishers are using them anyway.
How it started
Long before ChatGPT became a thing, educators and editors frequently used anti-plagiarism tools to see if writers were being honest about their work. These tools work by comparing a written work against a database filled with content from across the web, scholarly articles, and more to check for matching sentences and phrases. Some, like Turnitin, offer a percentage that claims to illustrate how much of the student’s writing overlaps with other works. Between potential false positives and uncertainty about whether work was duplicated intentionally, some educators have backed away from using that particular tool.
But now, the hunt for copied content is evolving into a war on AI-generated work. As quickly as students have picked up ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, teachers have adopted so-called AI detectors just as fast. A survey from the Center for Democracy and Technology found that 43 percent of sixth to 12th grade teachers in the US regularly used AI detectors between 2024 and 2025. Some universities already using Turnitin in their learning management systems found that the service automatically enabled AI detection when the tool launched in 2023.
Instead of comparing pieces of written content, AI detectors like GPTZero, Pangram, and the one created by Turnitin rely on their own AI models to guess whether something might not be human-written — a process that’s arguably even murkier than matching text on the web. As noted by GPTZero, AI detectors use an algorithm to analyze a text’s wording, rhythm, and structure, as well as to pick up on patterns in length and tone that may be more common in AI-written text. This relatively subjective evaluation isn’t as solid as something you could back up by matching text online, and can get tripped up by writers who speak English as a second language. Despite this, Turnitin has said that its AI detector falsely flags less than 1 percent of human-written content as AI, while Pangram claims its false positive rate is just 1 in 10,000. GPTZero claims it has a similarly low rate of mistaking human content for AI.
How it’s going
People online are already accusing each other of “sounding like AI,” but the ready availability of AI detection tools is only adding fuel to the LLM witch hunt. In some high-profile cases, AI writing accusations have directly impacted people’s livelihoods and reputations. Last month, the publisher Minotaur dropped a $2 million book deal over concerns that its author, Jerry Falade, used AI — something he vehemently denies.
There’s Thierry Rignol, a French national who sued Yale last year after a professor accused him of writing portions of his final exam with AI, resulting in a failing grade and a one-year suspension. The professor used GPTZero to scan Rignol’s writing for signs of AI, but the lawsuit argues that “AI surveillance and detection tools are known to unfairly target non-native English speakers” like Rignol. In February, a student at Adelphi University won a lawsuit against the school after his professor similarly claimed he used AI to write an essay. Though the lawsuit doesn’t say which AI tool the professor used to examine the student’s essay, Adelphi University has a licensing agreement with Turnitin.
A 2023 Stanford study found that AI detectors falsely flagged essays written by non-native English speakers as AI more often than native speakers. (Many services still argue that their tools are accurate when dealing with text written by non-native speakers.) These tools may also be biased against neurodivergent writers.
As pointed out by the University of California, Los Angeles, AI detection tools are trained to pick up on patterns that could indicate AI use, such as repetitive terms and phrases, text that sounds too formal or informal, and nonsensical phrasing. Some, like QuillBot, also measure the “unpredictability” of text, as “AI tends to make the most ‘obvious’ or most common language choices as compared with human-produced writing,” according to UCLA. They may also look for sentence structure that remains the same throughout as another sign of AI. But these measurements aren’t indicative of AI on their own, as some people may just have a writing style with these qualities.
Even though Turnitin touts low false positive rates, it maintains that its tool “may not always be accurate” and shouldn’t be used to take actions against a student. Grammarly warns that users “should never rely on the results of an AI detector alone,” while GPTZero says “no AI detector can ever truly be 100% perfect.” OpenAI even shut down its own AI writing detector in 2023 due to low accuracy.
But AI writing accusations are still being flung across the web. Last week, in a video broadcast to the more than 3.5 million followers across his social channels, Ozzy Osbourne’s son, Jack, accused journalist and Verge contributor Kat Tenbarge of using AI to write an article for Rolling Stone, while flaunting the results from an AI detector, Getsolved, as “proof” of his claim. Tenbarge has refuted the claim in a video and a post on her website, but Osbourne hasn’t retracted his accusation or deleted the video, leaving Tenbarge to deal with the trolls.
There are numerous examples of false accusations, from writers to students, with many accusers failing to acknowledge the disclaimers that come along with some of these AI detection tools.
What happens next
The uncertainty surrounding AI detectors is enough for some educational institutions to stop using them altogether. Yale University, Johns Hopkins University, Vanderbilt University, Georgetown University, and others have disabled or restricted the use of AI detection tools. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology also warns that “AI detectors don’t work.”
Instead of relying on tools to weed out AI, many schools are encouraging educators to rethink their lessons. The University of Chicago, for example, suggests telling students to slow down their reading, breaking up longer writing assignments, and requiring students to reflect on their work. Stanford University says professors can consider holding assessments in classrooms, while MIT advises professors to leave room for students to disclose whether they used AI for help on an assignment, without penalty.
With AI becoming more prevalent in and outside the classroom, efforts to suss out what’s written by a human or a machine are ramping up as well. Some online platforms are only exacerbating suspicions surrounding AI use. Substack has built Pangram into its app, allowing users to scan blogs for suspected AI-generated content, while LinkedIn added a “seems like AI slop” button on posts. The result is a new era of distrust, where readers constantly question whether what they’re reading is AI and real human writers try their best not to sound like it.
By the way
- The Authors Guild is helping writers get ahead of accusations by giving them “Human Authored” certifications. There are also Not by AI and Written by Human badges users can add to their work online.
- Wikipedia created a guide to help editors spot AI writing, which includes looking for writing that “puffs up” the importance of a topic or provides “superficial analysis of information.” The site has also banned AI-generated articles.
Read this
- The New York Times has a fun quiz that asks you to look at five pairs of passages and choose which blurb you like better — the catch is that one of them is written with AI.
- Inside Higher Ed spoke to some educators about how they’re approaching AI in school, with one lecturer raising concerns about the costs and resources that could go into AI-proofing assignments.
- My colleague Jess Weatherbed detailed how the fanfiction community is having its own internal struggle over how to determine which stories are generated by AI.

articles.title: How to use ChatGPT's new, more natural Voice Mode for conversations - Engadget
articles.text:
How to use ChatGPT's new, more natural Voice Mode for conversations
Talking to ChatGPT just got a lot less awkward.
AI assistants like ChatGPT have been advancing at a steady rate, offering more capabilities, better accuracy and faster responses with each new model. Generative AI is not perfect, and you really shouldn't see it as an unquestionable source of information, but for those who have embraced the technology, it might be more convenient to switch to voice conversations instead of typing everything out. ChatGPT's original Voice Mode in 2023 relied on three separate systems to make it work. It would first convert your speech into text, generate an answer using a language model and then use a text-to-speech model to read it aloud.
The Advanced Voice Mode came after and featured a single multimodal model that improved things considerably. ChatGPT now ships with the GPT-Live model for handling voice conversations, and it is a major step up in terms of how natural the conversations feel. OpenAI calls it a "full-duplex" architecture that allows it to listen and speak at the same time. This is a gripe you might have had with the previous voice model, which could sometimes mistake a brief pause for the end of your turn and start replying before you had actually finished your sentence.
You will now occasionally hear ChatGPT vocalizing short acknowledgements like "mhmm" or "yeah" while you're speaking, similar to how a person might respond during a real conversation. GPT-Live can also pass on more complex tasks to other capable models, like GPT-5.5, in the background when a question requires reasoning or research.
Starting a conversation with GPT-Live
The GPT-Live voice model is available through the ChatGPT app on Android and iOS devices and on the web through any browser. ChatGPT Pro, Plus and Go users will have access to the GPT-Live-1 model, while those on the free plan can access the GPT-Live-1 mini model. GPT-Live replaces the previous turn-based Advanced Voice model as the default option. To get started, simply tap the ChatGPT Voice icon, which is represented by a waveform symbol, at the far right of the text box. If this is your first time conversing with ChatGPT using your voice, you might be prompted to grant it access to your device's microphone.
Once you've entered voice mode, you'll see a responsive floating orb on the screen. You can now start talking as you normally would. If you tap on the settings icon at the top-right corner, you can change the intelligence of the voice model. You have three options to choose from: Instant, Medium and High. This customization is not available on the GPT-Live-1 mini model, so currently requires a paid plan. ChatGPT Voice will remain active even if you switch to another app or lock your device.
While the overall experience is an upgrade over the previous iterations of ChatGPT's voice mode, GPT-Live currently doesn't support screen or video sharing. Fortunately, you can revert to the older voice model by heading into ChatGPT's settings, navigating to Voice and selecting a different model. Here, you can also pick a different voice for ChatGPT, change its language or set ChatGPT Voice to be the default mode when you launch the app.
What GPT-Live excels at
I'm someone who prefers typing things out, so I hadn't given much thought to the upgraded version of ChatGPT Voice initially. Well, that is until I actually tried having a few long-drawn conversations with it. What impressed me the most wasn't its intelligence, but how quickly I stopped thinking about the fact that I was conversing with an AI. ChatGPT Voice no longer cuts you off mid-sentence, and you don't need to awkwardly wait for it to finish speaking before jumping back in. With longer queries, I could almost feel like GPT-Live could anticipate what I was going to say next.
GPT-Live's responsiveness makes it a great tool for carrying out live translations, too. At any time during your conversation with GPT-Live, you can scroll down to reveal the transcript of everything being said. If you ask ChatGPT a question that it thinks can be answered better with a visual, it will create an interactive widget alongside its spoken response.
GPT-Live's intelligence level is set to Instant by default, which handles most everyday questions with ease while prioritizing quick responses. It can still offload searches and deeper reasoning to the more capable models in the background while it keeps the conversation flowing. If you do plan on discussing complex topics with GPT-Live more regularly, I found that switching to the Medium and High intelligence levels adds a split second or two of extra thinking time, but the added delay doesn't take away from how naturally the conversation flows.

articles.title: These Earbuds Survived My Sweatiest Workouts
articles.text:
The best workout headphones disappear when you start moving. They’re locked in without readjustments and comfortable enough that the music feels like it’s coming from inside your head. Your workout headphones have a tougher job than your everyday pair. They need to survive sweat, being thrown into a gym bag, and the occasional drop. They also need to sound good enough to keep you motivated until the finish line.
The WIRED Reviews team has tested hundreds of headphones and earbuds, and I’ve narrowed down the models that best balance sound quality, comfort, and durability. We put these picks through workouts like weightlifting and indoor swimming, as well as outdoor activities like trail runs, hikes, and cycling, to evaluate which headphones enhanced the experience and which ones got in the way. This roundup includes a mix of headphones and earbuds, wired and wireless, from the top pick, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 ($250), to the bone-conduction Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 ($180).
For more recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Earbuds, the Best Open Earbuds, and the Best Bone Conduction Headphones.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Featured in This Guide
Best Wireless Earbuds for Working Out
Beats were the first sport earbuds to tap into Apple’s ecosystem, but the Powerbeats Pro 2 work nearly as well with Android, making them a great pick for any phone. The redesigned nickel-titanium ear hooks stayed in place through hours of testing, and former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata said they’re the most comfortable hooked earbuds he’s worn. The noise canceling is a major upgrade, outperforming the Beats Studio Buds+ and holding its own against premium rivals like Sony’s WF-1000XM5 and Technics’ AZ80. The Powerbeats Pro 2 also finally add a natural-sounding transparency mode, along with punchy sound, up to 10 hours of battery life (eight with ANC enabled), and convenient push-button controls.
Apple users get extras like iCloud device switching, Find My functionality, and hands-free Siri, while Android users still benefit from the Beats app, heart rate monitoring, and one-touch pairing. I wish the PowerBeats Pro 2 had a higher IP rating than IPX4, but they’re still built to handle sweat and light rain.
| Specs |  | 
|---|---|
| Battery Life | Up to 10 hours (8 hours with ANC enabled; Case holds an extra 35 hours) | 
| Durability | IPX4 | 
| Compatibility | iOS and Android | 
Best Wireless Headphones for Working Out
If you prefer over-ear headphones for your workouts, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 are hard to beat. The plush fit is comfortable enough for long listening sessions, and the impressive noise canceling blocks out any distractions at the gym. The sound is clear and engaging, with plenty of punch, plus a transparency mode that feels natural. Bose also added useful upgrades like USB-C lossless audio, improved ambient controls, and longer battery life.
The ear cups do trap heat and sweat, but I have yet to find a pair of over-ear headphones that don't encourage sweat during intense workouts. Nonetheless, they are a premium pick for anyone who wants workout headphones to double as everyday headphones.
| Specs |  | 
|---|---|
| Battery Life | Up to 30 hours | 
| Durability | No IP rating | 
| Compatibility | iOS and Android | 
Best Budget Buds
JLab’s Go Air Sport is the sport version of the insanely affordable Go Air, with a slight markup for over-ear hooks and a case with a cover. That case also has a built-in USB charger. The build quality is solid, and touch controls are not too sensitive; I don't accidentally turn off my music or turn up the volume whenever I adjust my hair or my hat. They have a solid 30 hours of battery life when you recharge them in the case. I wore them for two weeks for a few hours each day while running and walking my dog, and I didn't have to recharge them once. And the Bluetooth connection is stronger than most affordable earbuds I've tried; I don't have to be wary about walking around a corner, away from my phone. As a bonus, they also come in a wide array of playful colors. —Adrienne So
| Specs |  | 
|---|---|
| Battery Life | Up to 35 hours | 
| Durability | IP55 | 
| Compatibility | iOS and Android | 
Best Premium Earbuds
Bose is the undisputed king of noise-canceling headphones, so if you really need to lock in, consider the QuietComfort Ultra 2 Earbuds. According to former editor Parker Hall, the noise-canceling on the second-gen pair bested the competition and was better than its predecessor. You get wireless charging in the clamshell and guards to prevent earwax buildup. Bose uses a chiming calibration tool to adjust the sound profile and noise-canceling response to the shape of your actual ear canals, which is impressive. If you get too deep in the zone, there's also an Aware mode that lets you hear ambient noise while smoothing out loud sounds. Not only are these the best for the gym, but they're also probably the best pair for anyone who wants noise cancellation in a compact package that you can tote around every day. —Adrienne So
| Specs |  | 
|---|---|
| Battery Life | Up to 30 hours | 
| Durability | IPX4 | 
| Compatibility | iOS and Android | 
Best Earbuds for Apple Users
The AirPods Pro 3 are the first AirPods model I've used that I legitimately consider to be workout headphones. (Previous models fell out all the time.) Apple conducted what former WIRED editor Parker Hall calls “an ungodly number” of laser ear scans, and there is a greater choice of ear tips. The XXS small tips actually fit me well, and these are the first AirPods Pros that haven't fallen out of my ears while running.
Like the Powerbeats Pro 2, they also have heart rate sensing, so if you're tracking your workout with Fitness+ and using Workout Buddy, you can see your live heart rate in the app or on your Apple Watch. Noise canceling is also excellent if you're working out in the gym. Apple's bass-heavy, bright tuning is also ideal if you're bopping around to pop sensations like Haim or Mariah Carey when you're working out. —Adrienne So
| Specs |  | 
|---|---|
| Battery Life | Up to 8 hours with ANC, 24 hours with the case | 
| Durability | IPX4 | 
| Compatibility | iOS and Android | 
Best Earbuds for Running
The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 now charge via USB-C, so you can say goodbye to their proprietary charger. These earbuds use both air and bone conduction to transmit sound while you’re working out outside. This new model added a second air-conduction unit, which improves the sound quality and reduces the tingling sensation you get with bone conduction.
WIRED contributing reviewer Michael Sawh notes that the battery life is slightly less than promised, and the waterproof rating is lower than on previous iterations (IP67). According to Sawh, the sound quality isn’t as clear as one might like, but the bass and punch are still powerful. Former WIRED editor Adrienne So says these are her favorite pair of headphones for cycling because they fit comfortably underneath a helmet.

|---|---|
| Battery Life | Up to 12 hours | 
| Durability | IP55 | 
| Compatibility | iOS and Android | 
Best Earbuds for Swimming
The OpenSwim Pro has an industry-leading IP68 rating and a dedicated swimming EQ mode that produces a balanced sound that is pleasant to listen to underwater. According to WIRED contributing reviewer Michael Sawh, the controls are easy to use, and the neckband is slim enough to wear under a swim cap. Since Bluetooth doesn’t work underwater, you’ll need to import audio files from your computer onto your swim headphones. There’s 32 GB of onboard storage. Be sure to check the format to make sure it's compatible; the OpenSwim Pro supports MP3, FLAC, WAV, AAC, M4A, APE, and WMA files.

|---|---|
| Battery Life | Up to 9 hours | 
| Durability | IP68 | 
| Compatibility | iOS and Android | 
Best Wired Earbuds for Working Out
If you're running or hiking, it's convenient to have a pair of earbuds that are attached to you and won't fall into a puddle. Former WIRED editor Adrienne So loves these Soundpeats Q40HD, mainly because they’re designed with two clips to attach to your shirt; plus the buds themselves are magnetic and click together when not in use. In testing, Adrienne was able to get around 20 hours of battery life, and even when power is low, a quick top-off with a USB-C cable got her more than enough battery to last for an hour-long trail run. The headphones don't include active noise cancellation, but they fit well enough to provide passive noise cancellation. They block ambient sounds so well, in fact, that she only wears one bud when running.

|---|---|
| Battery Life | Up to 20 hours | 
| Durability | IP67 | 
| Compatibility | iOS and Android | 
Honorable Mentions
BlueAnt Pump X for $100: The BlueAnt Pump X has an incredible standout feature: cooling gel ear pads that you can keep in the fridge and swap out for the regular ear pads, so you don't get too sweaty. The single-button operation is intuitive, and ANC is effective. Battery life was also startlingly long—I wore them for an hour or two a day for several weeks before the battery got to 50 percent. The regular ear pads are soft and comfortable, and they're also water-resistant, which is unusual in over-ear gym headphones. There's also a special X Mode that pumps up the bass; I could feel distinct vibrations with my bass standard, Beyoncé's “Partition.” The price is also reasonable. —Adrienne So
Skullcandy Crusher 540 Active for $210: The BlueAnt headphones are just a better buy in all regards, but I enjoyed these a lot. The noise canceling doesn't work very well, but these headphones are attractive, and the bass is powerful. —Adrienne So
Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro’s sound quality is excellent; the buds are beautiful and comfortable; and I appreciate the physical buttons. That said, the open-ear noise-reduction system merely blunts outside noise rather than blocking it, so I don't understand the value here. —Adrienne So
Soundcore AeroFit 2 Pro for $180: The AeroFit 2 Pro physically switches modes with its adjustable ear hooks to transform from open earbuds to noise-canceling ones. Unfortunately, I found the case to be too big, and the noise cancellation wasn’t so effective. Still, it's an interesting concept, and I do like being able to toggle the angle on the ear hooks for a more secure fit. —Adrienne So
Oakley Meta Vanguard for $499: Not only are they Oakley sunglasses with Prizm lenses for enhancing contrast and keeping you from tumbling head over heels on the trail, but they also have a 12-MP action camera in the bridge of the nose, two over-ear speakers with a five-mic array for calls, and they integrate with Garmin to work as a (not very useful) fitness tracker. That's OK, because these are the best for moving at speed. They are 6 decibels louder than the Oakley Meta HSTNs, and you can tell. They're the only open headphones where I don't have to turn the volume all the way up to hear podcasts when going over 20 mph. —Adrienne So
Chamelo Music Shield for $260: Chamelo's audio sunglasses have electro-chromic lenses; you can change how dark they get with a finger slider on the arm. However, the music isn't very loud, the battery life is much worse than the Vanguard, and they're relatively expensive. —Adrienne So
JLab Epic Sport ANC 3 for $100: This is the upgraded version of the Go Air Sport above, with hybrid dual drivers for better sound, a higher IP rating, better battery life, and active noise canceling. You need a fully sealed fit for ANC to be effective, which these don't have; I can still hear people at the gym when I'm lifting weights. Still, in every other way, these headphones meet their promises, and they do feel secure. —Adrienne So
H2O Audio Tri 2 Pro Multi-Sport for $220: These are a huge improvement from the first iteration of the brand's waterproof headphones, thanks to a more secure fit, better buttons, and a smoother silicone finish. However, they're pricier than the Shokz, and they use a proprietary charger instead of USB-C. —Adrienne So
Nwm Go for $99: Stylish Japanese brand Nwm recently launched these open-ear bone conduction headphones that purport to reduce sound leakage. It works—they sound fine and are incredibly light; they also use a proprietary charger. —Adrienne So
Nothing Open Earbuds for $99: These are some of the slimmest buds I've tested, and they fit well under layers of hoods, helmets, and hats. —Adrienne So
JLab JBuds Mini for $40: For tiny earbuds, these sound pretty decent. They’re IP55, so they’re sweatproof and dustproof, and because they fit so well, the noise canceling is effective. The biggest drawback is that they’re not great for phone calls. They also only get around five hours of playtime without the case and 20 hours with it.
Suunto Sonic for $79: If you want to try a neckband-style headphone like the Shokz above, but for cheaper, WIRED contributor Michael Sawh says these are lightweight with a balanced sound profile. —Adrienne So
Speck Gemtones Sport for $70: These are cheap and fit well. The buttons are a little too sensitive, and the sound is noticeably fuzzier than most of our other picks, but they're not terrible. —Adrienne So
Avoid These Headphones and Earbuds
Raycon Bone Conduction Headphones for $100: These headphones were so uncomfortable, pressing on my ear canal where they buzzed the flesh of my eardrums and not my bones. It was unbearable. —Adrienne So
Skullcandy Method 360 ANC for $130: In testing, I found the earbuds and case to be huge. The noise canceling also doesn’t work at all. —Adrienne So
Anker Soundcore C40i for $120: These open-ear buds fell out before I'd run a block down my street. I put them in my pocket and didn't wear them again for the rest of the run. —Adrienne So
1More Fit Open for $55: These earbuds sound OK, but the buttons are so sensitive that I couldn't run for more than five minutes without a song skipping or the music turning off. —Adrienne So
